# Probability Simulation in R {.unnumbered} *This hour has one job: to show you that the thing the room built by hand and the thing R builds in a fraction of a second are the same object. You will run a lot of code and write almost none. That is deliberate. Code you cannot interpret is worse than no code at all, and the interpreting is the part that matters.* Work through the tasks in order. Predict before you run, every time. ## Setting up {#sec-setup} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: open the script and load the tub** :::: ::::{.task-container} Open `session-01.qmd` from the module workspace and run the two blocks below. The first attaches the tidyverse and the helper file that holds the bean population. The second builds the tub. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) source("R/sampling.R") beans <- bean_population() ``` ::: Then look at what you have made. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beans nrow(beans) ``` ::: You should have 800 rows, one per bean, with a `bean_id` and a `mass_g`. :::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## R knows something you did not In the room you could not weigh all 800 beans, so the population mean was mine to reveal. Here you can compute it whenever you like, and that is an artificial luxury. Real populations never let you check. For the rest of this hour, resist looking at `mean(beans$mass_g)` until a task tells you to. The exercise only works if the population mean stays unknown while you are estimating it. ::: ## One draw :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: reproduce your own hand** :::: ::::{.task-container} This is the code equivalent of reaching into the tub without looking, taking five beans, and putting them on the balance. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sample <- beans |> slice_sample(n = 5) my_sample mean(my_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: - Run it. Write the mean down. - Run the whole block again, and again. Write down the first four means you get. - Compare with the person next to you. Compare with what you got on paper in the last hour. - Write comments (using `#`) above each line of code as though you were explaining to another person what they do. Which line of code is producing the randomness?
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # This line of code changes each time it is run, drawing a random five samples from the larger beans population my_sample <- beans |> slice_sample(n = 5) # prints out the randomly drawn samples my_sample # calculates the mean of the sample mean(my_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: `slice_sample()`. It is the only line whose output changes between runs. `mean()` is entirely deterministic: give it the same five numbers and it returns the same answer every time. The randomness enters at the draw and is then carried through the arithmetic, which is exactly why the mean of a random sample is itself a random variable.
:::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## A thousand draws Doing by machine what the class did by hand, twenty-five times over. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: build a sampling distribution** :::: ::::{.task-container} Read the code first, then run it. `map_dbl()` repeats an operation and collects the answers into a vector of numbers; the `\(i)` is a shorthand for "for each repetition, do this". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1986) sampling_dist <- tibble( replicate = 1:1000, sample_mean = map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) mean(slice_sample(beans, n = 5)$mass_g)) ) sampling_dist ``` ::: Now plot it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(sampling_dist, aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) + labs(x = "Mean mass of 5 beans (g)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: :::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why `set.seed()` `set.seed()` fixes the starting point of R's random number generator, so that everyone in the room gets the same thousand samples and your figure matches mine. This is a convenience for teaching and for reproducible reports. It does not make the samples any less random in the sense that matters here; it makes them reproducibly random. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![One thousand sample means, each from a sample of five beans. The individual bean masses are shown pale behind, on the same axis. This is the object the room built forty times over.](01-computing_files/figure-html/fig-thousand-1.png){#fig-thousand width=672} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: put the room on top of the machine** :::: ::::{.task-container} `class_means.csv` holds the means the room generated in the previous hour, one row per student, in a column called `sample_mean`. Read it in and overlay it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class_means <- read_csv("data/class_means.csv") class_means ggplot(sampling_dist, aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70") + geom_rug(data = class_means, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) + labs(x = "Mean mass of 5 beans (g)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: Each black tick is one person in this room. Where do they sit relative to the simulated distribution? Are there any ticks in a place the simulation says should almost never happen? :::: ::: ## Changing the sample size {#sec-changing-n} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: predict, then change the sample size** :::: ::::{.task-container} Before you touch the code, write down two predictions for what happens to the histogram when `n = 5` becomes `n = 20`: 1. What happens to where it is centered? 2. What happens to how wide it is? Now change both `5`s in the `slice_sample(beans, n = 5)` line and rerun. Then do it again with `n = 50`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1988) sampling_dist_20 <- tibble( replicate = 1:1000, sample_mean = map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) mean(slice_sample(beans, n = 20)$mass_g)) ) ggplot(sampling_dist_20, aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) + labs(x = "Mean mass of 20 beans (g)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Check the axis before you conclude anything `ggplot()` rescales the axes to fit whatever you give it, so a narrower distribution can be drawn looking exactly as wide as a broader one. Read the numbers on the horizontal axis of each plot, not the shape. To compare honestly, fix the axis with `+ xlim(0.2, 1.0)` on all three. ::: :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same population sampled at three sample sizes, on a common axis. The centre does not move. The width shrinks, and it shrinks by less than you might expect between 20 and 50.](01-computing_files/figure-html/fig-three-n-1.png){#fig-three-n width=672} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: now look at the answer** :::: ::::{.task-container} Only now, compute the thing you have been estimating all hour. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(beans$mass_g) ``` ::: Compare it with the centre of each of your three histograms, and with the single sample mean you got from your very first draw. :::: ::: ::: {.webex-check .webex-box} As the sample size goes up, the sampling distribution gets narrower. As the sample size goes up, the sampling distribution moves closer to the population mean.
It is worth being careful here, because the false answer is intuitive. The distribution does not *move*: it was always centred on the population mean, at every sample size, including n = 5. What changes is its width, so any *individual* sample mean is likely to land closer. The centre is already right; the spread is what improves.
Going from n = 5 to n = 20 made the sampling distribution
::: ## Sampling bias You have just established that a bigger sample gives a better estimate. That is true, it is the most useful thing in the session, and it holds under one condition that has been quietly in place since the workshop began. In the room you were told to look away from the tub, and to put the beans back if you caught yourself choosing. `slice_sample()` has been doing the same thing for you ever since. Real sampling is often not like that, and rarely because anyone cheated. Bigger beans are easier to pick up. Bolder animals walk into traps. Healthier plants survive to be measured. Patients who feel worse do not come back for the follow-up. In each case something **about the thing being measured also affects its chance of being measured**. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: Build a biased sample method** :::: ::::{.task-container} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} truth <- mean(beans$mass_g) blind_mean <- function(n) { beans |> slice_sample(n = n) |> pull(mass_g) |> mean() } ## weight by tells slice_sample() to make heavier rows more likely to be sampled grabbed_mean <- function(n) { beans |> slice_sample(n = n, weight_by = mass_g) |> pull(mass_g) |> mean() } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1988) comparison_5 <- bind_rows( tibble(sample_mean = map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) blind_mean(50)), method = "Blind draw"), tibble(sample_mean = map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) grabbed_mean(50)), method = "Grabbed") ) ggplot(comparison_5, aes(x = sample_mean, fill = method)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") + geom_vline(xintercept = truth, linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "Mean mass of 50 beans (g)", y = "Count", fill = NULL) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: :::: :::
::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-computing_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
If the procedure is biased, doing it again reproduces the bias exactly, every time. A larger sample then will just estimate the wrong quantity more precisely. It is hard, if not impossible, for statistics to correct a flawed sampling method! ## Stretch task Only if you have finished everything above with time to spare. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: break the population** :::: ::::{.task-container} The bean population is mildly right-skewed. Replace it with something far worse and see whether the sampling distribution notices. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1988) # A deliberately horrible population: most values near zero, a long right tail nasty <- tibble(value = rexp(800, rate = 2)) ggplot(nasty, aes(x = value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) + theme_minimal() nasty_means <- tibble( sample_mean = map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) mean(slice_sample(nasty, n = 30)$value)) ) ggplot(nasty_means, aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: The population is nothing like a bell. What shape are the means?
::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-computing_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-computing_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-2.png){width=672} ::: :::
There is a name for what you have just seen and a set of conditions under which it holds. Both are Session 2's, so do not go looking them up; bring the observation instead. :::: :::
